title: Turkey, light or dark meat, fried, coated, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird native to North America. The meat can be light (breast) or dark (thighs, drumsticks). This product consists of turkey pieces that are coated and deep‑fried, with the skin removed before cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkeys were domesticated by Native Americans over 2,000 years ago.
Light meat contains less fat than dark meat, but both are high‑quality protein sources.
Deep‑frying creates a crispy crust while the coating locks in juices.
Turkey skin is often discarded for this preparation because it can become tough when fried.
In the United States turkey is strongly associated with Thanksgiving.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving of fried turkey provides about 25 g of high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Turkey contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and vitamin B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Lower cholesterol than red meat
items.content: Although frying adds fat, turkey generally has lower cholesterol than beef.

items.title: High fat and calorie content from frying
items.content: Deep‑frying increases calories and saturated fat, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird meat.

items.title: Risk of bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked turkey can harbor pathogens such as Salmonella.

items.title: Sodium in the coating
items.content: Pre‑made breadings often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fried coated turkey as a main dish, in salads, with sauces, or in sandwiches. Pair it with vegetable sides or whole‑grain products for a balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fried turkey in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.
